gap.reason: The introduction emphasizes insufficient understanding of how noble-metal elements and synthesis conditions govern NM-HEA formation and crystal structure, identifying the underlying formation mechanism as unresolved.

source_text:
High-entropy alloy (HEA) nanomaterials, comprising a minimum of five distinct elements, demonstrate both thermodynamic and kinetic stability propelled by a high-entropy effect. Their diverse composition and intricate surface atomic structures make them particularly adept at showcasing exceptional catalytic performance (1–9). Moreover, current research indicates that nearly all reported HEA nanomaterials incorporate noble metal elements. Given the widespread use of noble metals and their alloys in electrocatalysis, the emergence of noble metal–based HEA (NM-HEA) nanomaterials holds a pivotal role in future applications (3–24). These materials exhibit remarkable performance and substantial potential across various catalytic domains, leveraging the advantageous properties of both NMs and HEA (25). Their applications span a wide spectrum, including NH3 decomposition (4), NH3 oxidation (5), electrolytic water hydrogen evolution (7, 10, 11), oxygen evolution and reduction (12–17), CO2/CO reduction (18, 19), and methanol and ethanol oxidation (20–23). Nowadays, there are already many ways to synthesize NM-HEA nanomaterials, such as the carbothermal shock method, fast moving bed pyrolysis strategy, microwave heating method, polyol method, dealloying method, etc. (26, 27), but devising a straightforward, cost-effective, and scalable synthesis route for NM-HEA nanomaterials remains a persistent challenge. Moreover, comprehending the formation mechanism of NM-HEA nanomaterials, especially the role played by NM elements, holds paramount importance in tailoring their composition and structure. Notably, there is a paucity of research in this area, particularly regarding NM. Previous studies in our group have demonstrated the crucial role of platinum in the formation of Pt-based HEA nanomaterials, showing that the addition of Pt facilitated the creation of a single-phase solid solution [face-centered cubic (fcc)] when combined with other metals (23, 24). In contrast, systems lacking Pt, such as CoNiFe and CoCuNiFe nanoparticles, exhibited phase separation, element segregation, uncontrolled micromorphology, and high thermal decomposition temperatures. Hence, investigating the fundamental mechanism of NM elements (Pt, Ru, Ir, Pd, etc.) in the formation process of NM-HEA nanomaterials holds immense great meaning and presents a challenging frontier.

Besides, the precise manipulation of crystal structures at the atomic level within single nanoparticles is of great importance in expanding application spaces and enhancing performance, because diverse crystal structures formed by the same elements may react at different rates in identical reactions because of the varying binding energy across distinct crystal surfaces (28–31). Despite this significance, factors influencing the crystal structure of alloys remained scarcely explored, primarily because controlling the crystal structure of an alloy with an identical composition poses an exceptionally challenging task (32–35). While numerous studies have delved into single-phase solid solution in NM-HEA nanoparticles, a rational strategy to selectively control their crystal structures is not reported and well developed yet (3, 8, 36). This challenge is amplified in NM-HEA because of the complexity arising from multiple interacting elements (more than five) and intricate synthesis conditions involving rapid heating and cooling rates. Unlike simpler alloys with fewer elements, the complexity of NM-HEA makes achieving crystal structure control notably more demanding. Moreover, it is deemed that a higher count of atoms with different crystal structures exposed on the surface within the same nanoparticle enhances catalytic reactions (2, 3, 6, 25–27). Consequently, investigating methods to precisely design and control specific crystal structures, while maximizing the exposure of surface atoms, becomes inevitable for the advancement and application of NM-HEA nanomaterials.

queries.broad: For noble-metal–based high-entropy-alloy nanomaterials used in catalysis, what single, testable hypothesis identifies an intervention that could improve crystal-structure control and surface-atom exposure relative to an otherwise comparable baseline? State the proposed intervention, its mechanism, the predicted relative outcome, the conditions under which it should and should not work, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive experiment that could falsify it.
queries.problem_constrained: Starting from fixed-composition, single-phase solid-solution noble-metal–based high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles containing at least five interacting elements, what single intervention could overcome the current inability to selectively control crystal structure at identical composition while maximizing surface-atom exposure under synthesis conditions involving rapid heating and cooling? Formulate a testable hypothesis specifying the mechanism, the predicted structural and catalytic outcomes relative to same-composition nanoparticles prepared without the intervention and tested in an identical reaction, the relevant synthesis and test boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.
queries.expert_context: Existing synthesis approaches for noble-metal–based high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles include carbothermal shock, fast moving-bed pyrolysis, microwave heating, polyol synthesis, and dealloying, yet a straightforward, cost-effective, scalable route remains unresolved. Prior studies have largely focused on obtaining single-phase solid solutions, while the formation mechanism remains poorly understood and no rational strategy has been established for selectively controlling crystal structure at fixed composition. The problem is complicated by interactions among more than five elements and by rapid heating and cooling, with the additional design requirement of maximizing exposed surface atoms for catalysis. Under these constraints, what single intervention could enable reproducible crystal-structure selection in a fixed-composition, single-phase solid-solution noble-metal–based high-entropy-alloy nanoparticle? State a testable hypothesis giving the intervention, formation mechanism, predicted structural and catalytic outcomes relative to an untreated same-composition baseline, scalability and synthesis/test boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

queries.broad: For noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanomaterials, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs reproducible formation of a defined crystal structure and why this matters for catalytic performance? State one controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the conditions under which the hypothesis should hold, relevant prior evidence, and an outcome that would falsify it.
queries.problem_constrained: Consider noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles containing more than five elements and targeted in a single-phase solid-solution state. Their crystal structure is difficult to control at fixed composition, while unsuccessful formation can involve phase separation, elemental segregation, uncontrolled particle morphology, and high thermal decomposition temperatures under synthesis regimes with rapid heating and cooling. What testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs formation and crystal-structure selection in this regime and why? Define a controlled intervention without specifying a technique, predict the observations relative to the initial single-phase baseline, identify the applicable compositional and processing boundaries, cite supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.
queries.expert_context: Noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles have been prepared by carbothermal shock, fast moving-bed pyrolysis, microwave heating, polyol, and dealloying approaches, but a straightforward, cost-effective, and scalable route remains lacking. Earlier work found that platinum-containing multimetallic nanoparticles could form single-phase fcc solid solutions, whereas Pt-free CoNiFe and CoCuNiFe nanoparticles showed phase separation, elemental segregation, uncontrolled morphology, and high thermal decomposition temperatures. More broadly, selective crystal-structure control at identical alloy composition remains poorly developed, especially for systems with more than five interacting elements subjected to rapid heating and cooling; useful structures must also retain substantial surface-atom exposure because different structures of the same elements can exhibit different catalytic rates. Given this evidence and these constraints, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the role of noble metal elements in nanoparticle formation and crystal-structure selection, and why? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a Pt-based single-phase fcc baseline, boundary conditions across noble metal–based systems, the prior observations supporting the hypothesis, and a decisive falsification criterion, without prescribing an experimental technique.
